main.title: Jak 3
main.subtitle: Beyond the walls of Haven City
main.summary: Jak 3 is Naughty Dog's 2004 action adventure for PlayStation 2, the closing chapter of its original Jak and Daxter trilogy. Banished from Haven City, the pair find refuge among the desert outcasts of Spargus. Off-road journeys, platforming and gun battles carry their search for answers back towards a city still at war.

cards.heading: Exile in the Wasteland
cards.text: Jak 3 is Naughty Dog's 2004 action adventure for PlayStation 2, the closing chapter of its original Jak and Daxter trilogy. Banished from Haven City, the pair find refuge among the desert outcasts of Spargus. Off-road journeys, platforming and gun battles carry their search for answers back towards a city still at war.

cards.heading: Crossing the desert
cards.text: The Wasteland gives driving a central role. Choose an off-road vehicle, cross rough ground and deal with attackers along the route. Each machine has its own handling, armour and jumping ability. The fast Sand Shark carries front-mounted guns, while the Dune Hopper can clear gaps that other vehicles cannot reach.

cards.heading: Changing the shot
cards.text: The Morph-Gun's modifications change how familiar weapons behave. The Blaster can gain a bouncing shot that ricochets between walls and enemies, or launch a hovering drone that fires from above. Switching modifications lets the player respond to a crowded room or a distant target, with the available ammunition limiting each choice.

cards.heading: Drawing on Light Eco
cards.text: Light Eco opens another set of abilities alongside Jak's dark powers. It can restore health, slow the world around him, raise a shield or let him take to the air. These powers draw from an Eco meter. Deciding when to use one can create the opening needed to cross a dangerous space or survive a difficult encounter.

main.title: Halo 2
main.summary: Halo 2 is a 2004 first-person shooter game developed by Bungie and published by Microsoft Game Studios for the Xbox.

cards.text: Halo 2 is a 2004 first-person shooter game developed by Bungie and published by Microsoft Game Studios for the Xbox. The second installment in the Halo franchise, the campaign follows the supersoldier Master Chief and the disgraced alien commander Arbiter in a 26th-century conflict between the United Nations Space Command, the genocidal Covenant, and the parasitic Flood.

After the success of Halo: Combat Evolved (2001), a sequel was expected and highly anticipated. Bungie found inspiration in plot points and gameplay elements that had been left out of their first game, including online multiplayer. A troubled development and time constraints forced cuts to the scope, including the removal of a more ambitious multiplayer mode, and necessitated a cliffhanger ending to the campaign mode. Among Halo 2's marketing was an early alternate reality game, "I Love Bees", that involved players solving real-world puzzles. The gameplay is similar to its predecessor, while featuring new weapons, enemies, vehicles, and gameplay elements, most notably dual wielding certain weapons. Online multiplayer was available via Microsoft's Xbox Live service.

Halo 2 became the original Xbox's best-selling game, with more than eight million copies, and its most popular Xbox Live title until Gears of War arrived almost two years later. The online play helped establish matchmaking, lobbies and clans as expected parts of a console service. Critics praised the multiplayer, audiovisual design and music, while the campaign's abrupt ending divided players. Bungie continued with maps and fixes before releasing Halo 3 in 2007. Windows Vista and the later Master Chief Collection brought Halo 2 to further hardware.

main.title: The Getaway: Black Monday
main.summary: The Getaway: Black Monday is a 2004 action-adventure video game developed by London Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: A London crime story
cards.text: The Getaway: Black Monday is a 2004 action-adventure video game developed by London Studio and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. It is a sequel to 2002's The Getaway. The Getaway: Black Monday is set in London, with new characters. A third game, described as a spin-off of the series and entitled Gangs of London, was released exclusively for the PlayStation Portable in 2006.

cards.heading: Three approaches to action
cards.text: Like its predecessor, The Getaway: Black Monday is an action-adventure game played from third-person view in which the player controls the two lead characters Ben Mitchell, who is a member of London SO19 and Eddie O'Connor, a boxer-turned-heister, in an open world as they carry out their missions for game progression. Both of the characters can perform a series of physical tasks such as walking, sprinting, rolling, shooting, driving and taking cover during a gunfight. Black Monday introduced new stealth-centered missions where players control Sam Thompson as she can sneak around more easily than Mitchell and O'Connor, being able to grasp and hang around the balconies and edges. The downside however is that she is unable to use firearms or melee for combat.

cards.heading: Building the city
cards.text: Black Monday builds its action around a recognisable London. The publisher's original press material names Regent Street, Trafalgar Square and Piccadilly Circus, alongside routes beneath the city and along the Thames. Its map shows how streets, bridges and neighbourhoods connect. The city is both a setting for the crime story and a place the player crosses on foot or in a vehicle.

cards.heading: Capturing the performances
cards.text: The performances begin with actors rather than finished digital characters. The original press disc includes photographs of performers wearing motion-capture equipment, with tracking markers and head-mounted microphones visible. Its production notes describe magnetic and optical capture and facial animation. These photographs show part of that process; the equipment and people remain visible before their movements become a scene in the game.

cards.heading: Driving through London
cards.text: Cars and motorcycles share the streets with the characters. The sequel adds motorcycles and revises vehicle dynamics and damage, while its missions combine driving with action on foot. A production photograph shows two performers seated in a simple capture rig. It is a useful contrast with the finished street scenes: a few physical supports give the actors a position to work from before the surrounding vehicle and city appear on screen.

cards.heading: Orchestra and Ninja Tune
cards.text: The music combines an original orchestral score with urban remixes. The contemporary press sheet names Ninja Tune artists Amon Tobin, Diplo, Blockhead and Lotek. The press disc also includes photographs from an orchestral recording session: musicians, stands, microphones and a mixing desk. Together these materials show two sides of the game's sound, the recorded ensemble and the electronic contributions.

cards.heading: Three lives, different routes
cards.text: The crime story is told through different characters over a 48-hour period. Mitch is a police officer returning to duty; Eddie is a boxer caught up in a bank robbery; Sam is a thief whose missions emphasise avoiding confrontation. Choices lead to different routes and endings. Beyond the main story, the press material also describes free roaming, street racing, taxi driving and a tourist mode, giving players other ways to revisit the city.

main.title: Need for Speed: Underground 2
main.subtitle: Build a car, find a race
main.summary: Need for Speed: Underground 2 brings its tuner culture into Bayview, a city that players can drive through between races.

cards.heading: Build a car, find a race
cards.text: Electronic Arts announced Need for Speed: Underground 2 in North American stores on November 15, 2004. Its city of Bayview links five districts through streets and highways, putting events, shops and rivals along the player's route. Expanded customisation covers appearance and performance, while dyno tests support more detailed tuning. The soundtrack's Riders on the Storm remix featuring Snoop Dogg adds a distinctive musical entrance to its neon-lit streets.

cards.heading: The roads between events
cards.text: Driving between events gives players time to learn Bayview's roads, test changes to a car and find useful connections. Shops and garages occupy places to reach rather than only options in a menu. Free roaming extends the races into an explorable city, making knowledge of its districts useful during the next challenge.

cards.heading: A visual identity in the garage
cards.text: Bumpers, skirts, wheels, paint, vinyls, neon and audio systems provide extensive visual customisation. The game also evaluates visual impact and connects tuning to progression. Appearance becomes a continuing project alongside performance, turning the import and aftermarket culture of the period into a sequence of choices and rewards.

cards.heading: Test the setup on a dyno
cards.text: Gear ratios, suspension, aerodynamics and ECU settings can be adjusted for different events. Dyno graphs and tests show the effects of these decisions, allowing players to experiment with acceleration, stability and speed. Buying components supplies the parts; configuring them gives another way to prepare for a race.

cards.heading: An Outrun starts on the street
cards.text: Outrun challenges can begin with drivers encountered during free roaming. The goal is to pull far enough ahead of the opponent, with no fixed circuit to memorise. Intersections, traffic and knowledge of Bayview determine the route. Searching the city also reveals shops and other useful places, giving an unhurried drive its own rewards.

cards.heading: Riders on the Storm opens Bayview
cards.text: The soundtrack opens with a Riders on the Storm remix featuring Snoop Dogg, bringing the Doors song into the game's hip-hop and tuning setting. EA Trax supplies music across the garage, exploration and races. Repeated visits to those activities connect particular songs to the experience of building and testing a car.

cards.heading: Taking a build online
cards.text: Online racing on PlayStation 2, Xbox and PC let players test cars against human opponents. Vehicle choice, setup and appearance carried garage decisions into social competition. The feature extended the tuning theme beyond the career, offering another setting in which a personal build could be seen and driven.

main.title: Half-Life 2
main.summary: Half-Life 2 is a 2004 first-person shooter (FPS) game developed and published by Valve Corporation.

cards.heading: Physics joins combat and storytelling
cards.text: Half-Life 2 is a 2004 first-person shooter (FPS) game developed and published by Valve Corporation. It was published for Windows on Valve's digital distribution service, Steam. Like the original Half-Life (1998), Half-Life 2 combines combat, puzzles and storytelling, and adds features such as vehicles and physics-based gameplay. The player controls Gordon Freeman, who joins a resistance effort to liberate Earth from the alien Combine empire.

cards.heading: Building Source and a sense of presence
cards.text: Half-Life 2 was created using Valve's Source game engine, which was developed simultaneously. Development lasted five years and cost US $40 million. Valve's president, Gabe Newell, set his team the goal of redefining the FPS genre. They integrated the Havok physics engine, which simulates real-world physics, to reinforce the sense of presence and create new gameplay. They also developed the characterization, with more detailed character models and animations.

cards.heading: A missed deadline and a source-code leak
cards.text: Valve announced Half-Life 2 at E3 2003 with a release date of September of that year. They failed to meet the release date, leading to fan backlash. In October, the unfinished source code was published online, leading to more backlash and damage to the team's morale.

cards.heading: Steam release and a continuing influence
cards.text: Half-Life 2 was released on Steam on November 16, 2004. It won 39 Game of the Year awards and, like its predecessor, has been cited as one of the most influential FPS games and among the greatest games ever made. It was ported to the Xbox, the Xbox 360, the PlayStation 3, macOS, and Linux. By 2011, it had sold 12 million copies. Half-Life 2 was followed by the free extra level Lost Coast (2005) and the episodic sequels Episode One (2006) and Episode Two (2007). In 2020, after canceling Episode Three and several further Half-Life projects, Valve released a prequel, Half-Life: Alyx.

features.title: Build the tool beside its user
features.summary: A production method shapes the playable world.

cards.heading: A small level changes the direction
cards.text: Ken Birdwell's 1999 account of Half-Life describes a prototype assembled from the promising parts of an unsatisfying game. A small group put working ideas into one level, kept the enjoyable variations and cut others. A new software feature had to become something practical enough to build quickly. Playing that shared result gave the wider team a direction it could recognize. The prototype was therefore more than a demonstration for someone outside the studio: it helped colleagues discover what they wanted the rest of the game to become.

cards.heading: A feature needs someone to use it
cards.text: Birdwell also advises programmers to work directly beside artists while introducing technology into a sample part of the game. Watching what someone attempts can reveal where an interface needs simplification, documentation or another capability. He then suggests letting that artist demonstrate the result to colleagues. The account treats adoption as part of building a useful tool. A feature can exist in code without yet becoming something a team understands, trusts and regularly uses to create the places a player will eventually encounter.

cards.heading: The group has a demanding customer
cards.text: The later Half-Life 2 production account describes several small design groups rather than one central group. Each included programmers and level designers who depended on one another's work, including an engine programmer able to supply required technology. Sharing an office helped them decide which requests mattered most. The authors describe those relationships as a way to keep practical customers close to the people building a system. A proposed capability could be examined against the level that needed it instead of waiting for a distant handover.

cards.heading: Several crafts meet in one level
cards.text: Artists, acting specialists and sound production also had to meet those groups inside the levels. The 2005 account describes provisional sounds supporting prototypes before the final treatment followed a more stable design. Acting work supplied goals, rewards and animation, with some story-heavy spaces receiving their own design attention. These stages did not make each craft independent. A changed encounter could affect a model, a line or a sound, so the playable level became the place where several kinds of work had to function together.

main.title: Tekken 5
main.summary: Tekken 5 is a 2004 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades, before being ported to the PlayStation 2 in 2005.

cards.heading: Tekken 5
cards.text: Tekken 5 is a 2004 fighting game developed and published by Namco for arcades, before being ported to the PlayStation 2 in 2005. It is the fifth main game in the Tekken series, marking the tenth anniversary of the series. The game is set shortly after the events of Tekken 4 featuring a new antagonist named Jinpachi Mishima taking over the Mishima Zaibatsu while a sidestory focuses on the protagonist Jin Kazama as he faces several enemies from the G Corporation. The home version also contains a collector's edition of sorts, as it includes the arcade versions of Tekken, Tekken 2, Tekken 3, and StarBlade.

cards.heading: Customising the fighters
cards.text: The game reverts several major gameplay changes introduced in Tekken 4, such as uneven stage terrain, in favor of a more fluid gameplay akin to the older games in the series. It is also the first game in the series to feature the ability to customize characters with accessories, clothing, and other aesthetic items purchased with in-game currency. There are 32 fighters to choose from, including five new fighters as well as Jin's alter-ego Devil Jin.

cards.heading: Balance updates and Dark Resurrection
cards.text: The arcade version of the game was upgraded to Tekken 5.1 exclusively for the NAMCO 256 system on July 14, 2005, which had mostly balance changes to the gameplay including removing the infamous Double Stinger infinite combo of Steve Fox. It was then followed up with the final update Tekken 5: Dark Resurrection which was released in 2005 and later ported to the PlayStation Portable (as Tekken: Dark Resurrection) and the PlayStation 3. Tekken 5 was a critical and commercial success, selling over 9.43 million copies. Critics praised the return of classic gameplay features and the large amount of replay value provided by the PlayStation 2 port though the final boss Jinpachi Mishima was criticized for being too powerful, while Jin's mini-game story mode Devil Within was perceived as "boring" in comparison to the fighting game main Story mode which was open to every character. The sequel entitled Tekken 6 was released in 2007.

main.title: Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater
main.summary: Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater is a 2004 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater is a 2004 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the PlayStation 2. Written, produced and directed by Hideo Kojima, the game is the fifth mainline installment in the Metal Gear series and the first chronologically, serving as a prequel to the entire series. Set in 1964, the story centers on the FOX operative codenamed Naked Snake as he attempts to rescue Russian rocket scientist Nikolai Sokolov, sabotage the experimental superweapon Shagohod, and assassinate his defected former mentor, the Boss. While previous games were set in a primarily urban environment, Metal Gear Solid 3 adopts a 1960s Soviet jungle setting. Multiple new gameplay elements are added to match the setting, most notably camouflage, a new CQC combat system, player stamina that can be replenished by eating scavenged food, and an injury and treatment system.

Initially supposed to be developed for the PlayStation 3, Kojima moved development to the PlayStation 2 due to the long wait for the console. The jungle setting was difficult to develop for the game, requiring a new collision engine and planned features to be cut. Harry Gregson-Williams and Norihiko Hibino returned from Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty (2001) to compose the score, with the latter writing the game's opening theme, "Snake Eater". The game was released in late 2004 in North America and Japan, and in early 2005 in Europe and Australia. An expanded edition, titled Metal Gear Solid 3: Subsistence, was released in Japan in late 2005, then in North America, Europe and Australia in 2006; this version notably added a third-person camera to the main game and the online multiplayer component Metal Gear Online.

Metal Gear Solid 3 was met with critical acclaim, with many considering it an improvement over Sons of Liberty. Critics praised the narrative, characters, survival elements, and graphics, but some of the new gameplay mechanics and dated camera system were met with a more mixed reaction; the later Subsistence version would be praised for rectifying these issues. The game was also a commercial success, selling more than four million copies worldwide, and has since been considered one of the greatest video games of all time. A numbered sequel, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots, was released in 2008, while a narrative sequel, Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, was released in 2010. A remaster was included in the Metal Gear Solid HD Collection (2011), which was rereleased in the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 1 (2023) compilation. A remake, Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater, was released in 2025.

main.title: Mario Party 6
main.subtitle: The same board after sunset
main.summary: Mario Party 6 is Hudson Soft's GameCube party game, first released in Japan on 18 November 2004.

cards.heading: The same board after sunset
cards.text: Mario Party 6 is Hudson Soft's GameCube party game, first released in Japan on 18 November 2004. Its boards change between day and night, giving the usual race for Stars a visible cycle. Brighton and Twila represent the sun and moon as the gathering moves through different conditions. Players still roll dice, use items and compete in minigames, but a place seen earlier may work differently when reached again. The board becomes something to remember across time as well as a route towards the next prize.

cards.heading: Plan for the next change of light
cards.text: The light changes every three turns, altering spaces, characters and some minigame conditions. A useful route can therefore depend on when a player expects to arrive. Orbs provide effects to use or place around the board, and their importance extends to the final bonus awards. The day-and-night system gives decisions a shared clock: everyone can see the coming change, but a dice roll or another player's item may upset the timing of a carefully planned arrival.

cards.heading: A microphone joins the controllers
cards.text: The game introduced a GameCube microphone accessory for dedicated voice-controlled activities, adding another form of input to the party. Other minigames retain controller-based movement and reactions, making the microphone one part of a broader collection rather than the only way to take part. Hironobu Yahata and Shinya Outouge composed the score. The most distinctive change remains the board's cycle, which gives a familiar party structure a sense of passing time and lets the same themed location produce another situation when darkness falls.

main.title: Viewtiful Joe 2
main.summary: Viewtiful Joe 2, known in Japan as Viewtiful Joe 2: Secret of the Black Film, is a 2004 beat 'em up game developed by Clover Studio and published by Capcom for the GameCube and PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Viewtiful Joe 2
cards.text: Viewtiful Joe 2, known in Japan as Viewtiful Joe 2: Secret of the Black Film, is a 2004 beat 'em up game developed by Clover Studio and published by Capcom for the GameCube and PlayStation 2. The game's story begins where the original Viewtiful Joe left off, with the beginning of an alien invasion of Movieland by a villainous organization called "Gedow". The group is led by an unseen being known as the "Black Emperor", who proclaims his goal to collect the special Rainbow Oscars, seven statuettes which contain the "power of the happy ending". Straight from their previous adventure, superhero Viewtiful Joe and his girlfriend Sexy Silvia quickly charge themselves with stopping Gedow's evil plans.

cards.heading: Joe and Silvia manipulate the action
cards.text: Very similar to its predecessor, Viewtiful Joe 2 is a combination of 2D and 3D cel-shaded graphics with action, platforming, and beat 'em up gameplay elements. Using either of the characters Viewtiful Joe or Sexy Silvia, the player must utilize "VFX Powers" in order to battle enemies and solve puzzles. An integral part of the gameplay, these special abilities include being able to slow down, speed up, zoom into, or replay the onscreen action. Also akin to the original game, Viewtiful Joe 2 sold modestly but garnered considerable praise from critics due to its stylish graphics and gameplay.

main.title: Nintendo DS
main.subtitle: Two screens to rethink how we play
main.summary: Nintendo's dual-screen handheld combined a touchscreen, microphone and wireless play with traditional buttons and Game Boy Advance compatibility.

cards.heading: Two screens and a touch interface
cards.text: The Nintendo DS is a foldable handheld game console developed by Nintendo and released worldwide between 2004 and 2005. The "DS" in the name is an initialism for "Dual Screen", reflecting the system's most distinctive feature: two LCD screens working in tandem, with the lower screen functioning as a touchscreen. Both screens are housed in a clamshell design similar to that of the Game Boy Advance SP and some models of the Game & Watch series. The DS was among the first portable consoles to support wireless connectivity for local multiplayer over short distances, as well as online play through the now-defunct Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection service. Its primary competitor during the seventh generation of video game consoles was Sony's PlayStation Portable.

cards.heading: Dividing the view
cards.text: The two screens let developers separate action from maps, inventories or commands. They can also reverse those roles or distribute one scene vertically. Information that would cover the action on a single display can remain visible elsewhere. Each game has to decide how to guide attention between the surfaces, making the physical arrangement part of its design.

cards.heading: Point, draw and write
cards.text: The lower touchscreen lets players point, draw, drag and write with a stylus. Traditional buttons remain available alongside these gestures. WarioWare: Touched! and Super Mario 64 DS offered different uses at the Japanese launch, showing how touch could complement familiar controls or provide the basis for short activities of its own.

cards.heading: PictoChat connects nearby players
cards.text: Built-in PictoChat allows nearby systems to exchange text and drawings through local wireless communication. No cartridge is needed. The screens separate message history from composition, while the stylus supplies handwriting and sketches. Its short-range connection turns a group of handhelds in the same place into an improvised shared messaging room.

cards.heading: A slot for Game Boy Advance
cards.text: The original DS includes a slot for Game Boy Advance cartridges. Owners can continue playing much of their existing library while trying software designed for two screens and touch input. GBA games retain their original design and some functions depend on the hardware, but the extra slot gives the new handheld a practical connection to its predecessor.

sources.title: Nintendo DS
sources.attribution: Complete English Wikipedia introduction paragraph reproduced verbatim; heading supplied editorially.

features.title: Two windows onto play
features.summary: A screen changes who can look.

cards.heading: Two views of one situation
cards.text: Before the Nintendo DS launched, Satoru Iwata offered a simple example for its two displays. In an interview published in July/August 2004, he imagined a football game with an overview of the pitch on one screen and a character's view on the other. The example described an intention rather than naming a finished title. Two windows could let a player compare scales without replacing one image with another. The physical arrangement offered designers a way to make those different kinds of attention coexist.

cards.heading: A proposal beyond the specification
cards.text: Iwata placed that proposal inside a broader concern about games becoming too complicated. He wanted new experiences that people could understand without exhausting their time and energy. Asked about competing hardware, he resisted the idea that newer technology alone made entertainment better. The DS's extra display therefore belonged to an argument about what software might ask a player to do. In this contemporary interview, the president was setting out a design ambition, with the machine's eventual audience and uses still to be discovered.

cards.heading: Try the size on a piece of card
cards.text: For the later Nintendo DSi XL, the design conversation began with paper. Masato Kuwahara remembered cutting card to the proposed size and sketching screens on it. Yoneyama explained that panel cost depended on how efficiently individual displays could be cut from a larger sheet. The team found a workable size of 4.2 inches. A handheld's dimensions emerged from a meeting between a rough object someone could imagine holding and the economics of manufacturing its picture, well before a finished case reached a shop.

cards.heading: Leave it where somebody might look
cards.text: Larger screens also changed the machine's place in a room. In the DSi XL conversation, the team wanted an object people would leave on the table for another family member to pick up. Design research included visits to furniture shops. Wide-viewing-angle displays made the image clearer from the side, supporting a different kind of encounter with a handheld. The improvement was about more than one owner's private view: size, finish and visibility could help the machine remain inviting when it was resting between uses.
